Customer to share 3 representative eval prompts and sample traffic patterns by 2026-06-04
Schedule a 90-min technical deep dive with infra + SE to run initial benchmark (week of 2026-06-07)

summary: Polaris Labs currently uses OpenAI for generation and is exploring migration to Redwood Dedicated to reduce token costs and gain control over latency and data residency. They care about eval parity, easy compatibility with their vLLM/TGI stack, and enterprise security (VPC, KMS, SOC2). Next step is pricing + pilot benchmarks.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-30
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Ethan Moore (CTO, Polaris), Priya Singh (ML Eng), Rashid Khan (Infra)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, Diego my SE is here as well. Ethan, Priya, Rashid, thanks for making time.
[00:12] Ethan Moore: Yeah thanks Maya, appreciate it. Quick context — we're Polaris Labs, we run a customer-facing insights product that uses fairly heavy LLM generation for summarization and question answering. Right now we're on OpenAI, um hoping to evaluate Dedicated from Redwood to control costs and meet some latency SLAs.
[00:29] Diego Alvarez: Great, thanks Ethan. Can you share rough numbers — tokens per month, percent realtime requests vs batch, and latency targets?
[00:38] Priya Singh: Sure — we're at about 1.2B tokens/month, roughly 70% realtime (user-facing chat/summaries) and 30% batch offline jobs. Target p99 latency for user flows is <= 300ms for short responses (under 256 tokens).
[00:54] Rashid Khan: And infra-wise we need VPC peering and KMS integration for keys, plus SOC2 reports. Data residency in US only please.
[01:06] Maya Chen: Totally understood. Redwood Dedicated supports VPC/private deployments and KMS — Diego will cover details. Quick qualification — are you running any custom finetuned models or using base OpenAI models?
[01:18] Priya Singh: We're mostly using gpt-4 style for summaries and gpt-4o-ish for chat, nothing custom-finetuned yet, but we do run evals and some adapter-style tweaks with vLLM locally — question on compatibility there.
[01:31] Diego Alvarez: Good note. Redwood's runtime supports standard OpenAI-compatible APIs for many model variants; for vLLM/TGI workloads we provide deployment options and kernel/quantization guidance. There can be some differences in tokenization and subtle eval drift — we recommend a small eval suite during pilot.
[01:52] Ethan Moore: When you say OpenAI-compatible API, does that mean minimal code changes for us? Our product calls OpenAI endpoints directly from backend.
[02:00] Maya Chen: Usually it's a small swap — endpoint and auth change — and we offer SDKs and examples. For more complex tool-calling or function-calling flows Diego can help map the payload differences.
[02:12] Priya Singh: On the topic of evals — we ran a quick side-by-side with Anthropic and noticed some tricky hallucination modes. We need to ensure parity or at least measurable regression metrics.
[02:25] Diego Alvarez: Absolutely — we surface quality metrics and diff reports during pilot. For quantization/coming to Dedicated, sometimes 4-bit quantization or kernel selection affects rare token behaviors; we annotate those cases. We'll ask for a representative prompt set and some ground truth for the pilot.
[02:44] Rashid Khan: Can you run benchmarks that mimic our vLLM seq lengths? We often have 1k-2k token contexts for retrieval-augmented generation.
[02:53] Diego Alvarez: Yes we can — we'll need the traffic histogram (seq length distribution) and 95/99 percentiles. That helps choose GPU types and batching profiles.
[03:05] Ethan Moore: Pricing — main driver is token cost right now. OpenAI costs are creeping up, and our finance is pushing for committed pricing. How does Dedicated pricing work?
[03:16] Maya Chen: Dedicated is reserved capacity — commit to a GPU pool size and you get predictable throughput and lower per-token spend. There are also burst options for spiky traffic. We'll share a worksheet that maps your traffic to expected GPU hours and indicative cost.
[03:29] Priya Singh: What about auto-scaling? We can't have huge cold start latencies during traffic surges.
[03:35] Diego Alvarez: Dedicated supports configurable autoscaling with warm pools and fast warm-up; for strict p99 targets we recommend a baseline pool plus a modest burst reserve. Also caching/prefix KV cache can reduce load significantly on repeat queries.
[03:50] Ethan: When you say KV cache, do you mean Redwood's built-in prefix caching? We have our own LRU cache at app layer.
[03:58] Diego Alvarez: Yes — we provide optional prefix/KV cache that can be co-located on the same GPU nodes to avoid recomputation of past context. It's additive to your app-level cache.
[04:08] Priya Singh: On compatibility — we use an internal TGI/vLLM stack for some workloads. If we move inference to Dedicated, will we lose ability to run the same model code locally?
[04:18] Diego Alvarez: You can still run vLLM locally for experiments; Redwood Dedicated supports model variants and typically uses the same model file formats (transformer weights), but the runtime optimizations differ. There may be minor differences in sampling due to kernel changes — again, eval helps surface those.
[04:32] Rashid Khan: Security questions — SSO for team, RBAC for routes, audit logs, and customer-managed KMS.
[04:40] Maya Chen: All supported. We have SSO/SAML, role-based access controls in the Console, and audit logs. For KMS, we integrate with AWS KMS/HSM for key wrapping. We can provide SOC2 and pen-test reports.
[04:56] Ethan Moore: Good. Timeframe — ideally pilot in June and production by Q3 if benchmarks look good. Is that realistic?
[05:04] Maya Chen: Yes, that's a common timeline. Pilot to run 2-4 weeks for benchmark and eval parity checks, then expand.
[05:12] Priya Singh: One more — are there limits on model sizes or supported quantization formats? We're experimenting with 7B and 13B variants.
[05:20] Diego Alvarez: Supported — common 7B/13B/70B variants are fine. For aggressive quantization like 4-bit we do recommended profiles per GPU type. We'll propose model + quantization combos in the worksheet.
[05:34] Ethan Moore: Any known regressions vs OpenAI for generation quality?
[05:40] Diego Alvarez: Depends on model family — some open models can be close in many tasks but differ on instruction tuning and RLHF-like behavior. For strict parity we sometimes run a small fine-tune or instruction-tuning step; otherwise we monitor metrics and adjust decoding/hyperparams.
[05:58] Priya Singh: Sounds reasonable. For the pilot benchmarks, what do you need from us?
[06:04] Diego Alvarez: Minimal list: 1) representative prompt set (3-5k prompts ideally, or a sampled subset), 2) traffic histogram with seq lengths and qps over time, 3) a set of golden responses or evaluation rubric for QA/summaries. Also your current OpenAI latency/cost numbers for comparison.
[06:22] Priya Singh: We'll prepare those.
[06:25] Ethan Moore: On survivability — if Dedicated region goes down, can traffic failover to Redwood Hosted endpoints?
[06:32] Maya Chen: Yes — we support routing/fallback policies by region and capacity tier; you can set automatic fallback to hosted or another region.
[06:40] Rashid Khan: Does the private deployment still let Redwood staff access logs for support? We need to restrict that.
[06:47] Maya Chen: For Private/VPC models we can provide restricted access with just-in-time support controls and audit trail. We can scope access in the contract.
[06:55] Priya Singh: A couple of technical nitty-gritty — do you expose token-level cost breakdowns and per-route dashboards?
[07:02] Diego Alvarez: Yes, Redwood Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-model and per-route dashboards, tracing hooks, and error analysis.
[07:14] Ethan Moore: Ok can we see an example dashboard or a screenshot?
[07:18] Maya Chen: We'll share a deck and Console screenshots as part of the follow-up.
[07:24] Priya Singh: What about data retention and logging? We need logs for debug but can't retain user PII.
[07:31] Maya Chen: You can control retention and opt-out for user data; logs are configurable and we can support redaction or shorter retention windows.
[07:41] Ethan Moore: Let's talk costs briefly — if we move to Dedicated are there migration fees or just the committed fee?
[07:47] Maya Chen: Mostly commit fees; sometimes there's a small onboarding fee for private deployments if additional security review / custom networking required. We'll call that out in the worksheet.
[07:58] Priya Singh: On the integration side, do you support server-side streaming for responses? We rely on streaming for faster perceived latency.
[08:05] Diego Alvarez: Yes — streaming is supported. We also have a streaming SDK and can support function/tool calling semantics similar to OpenAI.
[08:14] Ethan Moore: Regarding model weights — do we need to provide any IP if we bring our own?
[08:20] Maya Chen: No, customers keep their model assets. For Redwood-hosted curated models we have licenses; for BYOM (bring your own model) we support loading weights into the Dedicated pool per contract.
[08:33] Rashid Khan: For the pilot, we'll probably start with a 13B quantized variant to keep costs low.
[08:39] Diego Alvarez: That's a common approach. We'll recommend GPU types for 13B quantized profiles in the worksheet.
[08:46] Priya Singh: Any gotchas with tokenization differences? We saw slight tokenization differences when moving from OpenAI tokenizer to some open tokenizers which changed prompt lengths and cost estimates.
[08:57] Diego Alvarez: Right — we'll include tokenization checks as part of the eval. Often the tokenizer is consistent with the chosen model's tokenizer, but when switching families there are differences.
[09:08] Ethan Moore: Can you support custom routes per org with different RBAC and quotas?
[09:13] Maya Chen: Yes — per-route and per-key quotas and RBAC rules can be set in the Console.
[09:21] Priya Singh: Great. Anything else on compliance? We need contractual clauses for data processing and incident response.
[09:28] Maya Chen: We'll send SOC2 and DPA templates; legal can align contract language in parallel.
[09:34] Ethan Moore: Ok, let's recap next steps. Maya?
[09:37] Maya Chen: Sure — we'll: 1) send Dedicated pricing worksheet and GPU recommendations by 2026-06-02; 2) Diego will send a benchmark plan and request list by 2026-06-01; 3) Polaris to share eval prompts and traffic histogram by 2026-06-04; 4) schedule a technical deep dive to kick off the pilot the week of 2026-06-07.
[09:59] Priya Singh: Sounds good.
[10:02] Ethan Moore: One last live question — do you have any existing customers who migrated from OpenAI to Redwood Dedicated with similar scale?
[10:09] Maya Chen: Yes — a few SaaS analytics customers at similar token volumes; we can share anonymized case studies and a reference if needed.
[10:17] Rashid Khan: We'll probably want a short reference check.
[10:20] Maya Chen: Happy to arrange.
[10:23] Ethan Moore: Thanks folks.
[10:26] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts.

Notes: Transcription occasionally mislabels speaker turns; there are minor tradeoffs discussed between quantization and eval parity; references to vLLM and TGI tokenization differences; shared artifact: benchmarking spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/polaris-proposed)
